Human sa nahitabo nga kaylap nga pagbaha sa dakong bahin sa Luzon niining bag-ohay nga mga adlaw, gimando ni Pangulong Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. ang hugot nga pagpatuman sa mga balaod nga may kalabotan sa urban planning, ilabi na sa mga kritikal nga lugar sa tibuok nasod nga kanunay gibahaan. Sa gipahigayon nga media conference niining Martes, Septyembre 1, miingon si Palace Press Officer Atty. Claire Castro nga kini nga paghugot sa pagpatuman sa balaod sa urban planning gihisgutan sa miting ni PBBM uban sa nagkalain-laing ahensya sa gobyerno nga nangita og solusyon sa dakong problema sa pagbaha sa Metro Manila ug ubang mga lugar. “Kung nasunod lamang daw ang mga ito ay maaaring ang mga lugar na dapat tayuan ng mga imprastraktura at mga lugar na bahain ang dapat manatiling libre at walang imprastrakctura para siya ang tumanggap ng tubig-ulan,” giit ni Castro. Matud niya, adunay mga master plan na sa urban development nga nahimo alang sa Metro Manila sukad pa niadtong 1941 ug 1956 alang sa Cebu apan wala kini mapatuman, hinungdan nga nakatukod og mga imprastraktura ug mga puy-anan sa mga lugar nga nakasamok sa hapsay nga pag-agos sa tubig gikan sa mga suba ug estero. “Huwag nang mamulitika. Ipatupad na ang batas. At dapat ipaliwanag sa lahat na maging istrikto sap ag-implementa ng batas para sa ating kaligtasan,” dugang niya. ============= Matapos naganap ang malawakang pagbaha sa malaking bahagi ng Luzon nitong mga nakaraang araw, ipinag-utos na Pangulong Ferdinand R. Dutertes Bring Comfort and Immediate Aid to Flood Evacuees in Bangkal DAVAO CITY – As floodwaters forced families to leave the safety of their homes on Friday evening, First District Representative Paolo "Pulong" Duterte and Vice Mayor Rodrigo "Rigo" Duterte II moved quickly to ensure that those affected were not left to face the ordeal alone. Continuous heavy rains caused a nearby creek to overflow, sending floodwaters into homes in Barangay Talomo and prompting local authorities to carry out a preemptive evacuation to keep residents safe. Through the Office of the First Congressional District and the Office of the Vice Mayor, immediate relief assistance was delivered to families taking shelter in evacuation centers, providing essential supplies to help them through the difficult night. Understanding that comfort can come from something as simple as a warm meal, Rep. Duterte and Vice Mayor Duterte also organized community cooking activities for evacuees at the Our Lady of Lourdes Central Park Gym and the Bangkal Satellite Gym in Royal Valley. Volunteers prepared and served freshly cooked meals, offering not only nourishment but also a sense of care and solidarity to families temporarily displaced by the flooding.

WAIST-DEEP FLOODWATERS IN KAWIT, CAVITE Residents were forced to wade through chest-deep floodwaters along Toclong-San Sebastian Road and Tramo Street in Barangay Gahak, Kawit, Cavite after a nearby river overflowed amid continuous monsoon rains on August 8, 2026. Residents said flooding has become a recurring problem whenever heavy rains hit the area, raising concerns over the river’s capacity to carry water during prolonged rainfall. Some residents also pointed to structures along the river, which they believe may be obstructing the natural flow of water and contributing to the flooding. They are calling on authorities to conduct an inspection of the river and surrounding structures, identify possible obstructions, and take appropriate measures to help prevent or reduce flooding in the community. As heavy rains continue, residents are urged to remain alert, avoid wading through floodwaters whenever possible, and follow advisories from local authorities.  Photos by Rene H. A SEA OF TRASH FLOODS THE RIVER BESIDE BACLARAN CHURCH A massive accumulation of garbage from Manila Bay filled the river in front of Baclaran Church in Parañaque City on Monday, August 10, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or Habagat swept debris into the area. The thick layer of floating waste created an alarming scene, with trash covering a large portion of the waterway. Nearby residents said they had never experienced anything like this before, highlighting the unusual scale of the debris buildup following the heavy rainfall. The incident once again raises concerns about waste management, waterways, and the impact of heavy rains on communities near Manila Bay. #1DNews | Davao, Philippines  FLOOD ALERT | Street Flooding Hits Carmelite Area in Bajada Following Hours of Rain LOOK: Residents of the Carmelite area in Bajada, Davao City, experienced street flooding early Wednesday, July 1, after several hours of continuous rainfall overnight. According to residents, flooding in the area is a recurring problem whenever heavy rains persist for more than two hours. As of this morning, floodwaters had reportedly risen from knee to waist level in some sections, affecting road access and threatening nearby homes, vehicles, and other properties. While residents noted that floodwaters typically recede within two to three hours after the rain stops, many continue to express concern over the recurring flooding and the damage it brings to their belongings and daily activities. Authorities are advising motorists and the public to exercise caution when passing through flood-prone areas. FOR THE NATION, NOT FOR DRAMA To our public servants in Congress: We don't need your tears. We need your receipts. The ₱7.2-trillion budget for 2027 belongs to every Filipino. It belongs to the farmer in Nueva Ecija, the fisherman in Samar, the OFW in Dubai, the jeepney driver in Cebu, and the teacher in Mindanao. It came from our taxes, our sweat, and our sacrifices. So instead of crying in the session hall, hold a press conference and tell the people:  "We approved your budget."  "Here is where every peso goes."  "Here is what your city and province will receive."  "We are ready to serve you in 2027." The House passed the ₱7.2-trillion budget on second reading on October 7, with ₱116 billion in amendments, and the final vote is set for Monday, October 12. Budget watchdogs are already warning that about ₱541.4 billion could go to "pork allocations". That is why the Filipino people are asking: WHERE IS THE MONEY GOING?  DPWH: ₱644 billion. Which roads, bridges and flood controls? Where, and when will they be finished?  Agriculture and agrarian reform: ₱276.57 billion. Will it reach our farmers?  DSWD: ₱241.56 billion. Will it reach the families who need it most? Our call is simple. POST THE BUDGET in every city hall, every provincial capitol and every barangay. Put it online, line by line, project by project. Let every Filipino see, check and monitor where the money goes. Transparency is not a favor. It is our right. Accountability is not optional. It is your duty. We don't pay taxes for tears. We pay for roads, schools, hospitals, jobs and our future. The people's money is for the people.  #Budget2027 #PeopleMoney #TransparencyNow #AccountabilityNow #ForTheNation #ProudFilipino See less FOR THE NATION, NOT FOR DRAMA

₱47-M Flood Control Project in Laoag Collapses — Ties Emerge Between  Contractor Linked to Davao Lawmaker and Sandro Marcos’ Office A newly built flood control structure along Padsan River in Barangay Gabu, Laoag City — a project worth ₱47,024,704.34 funded under the 2024 General Appropriations Act (GAA) — has collapsed JUST MONTHS after its reported completion, sparking fresh outrage over the alleged “flood-control mafia” operating in Congress. Photos taken on-site show large concrete revetments cracked, dislodged, and washed into the river, exposing reinforcing steel and leaving the riverbank vulnerable to further erosion.  The project billboard names RA Pahati Construction & Supply, Inc. as the contractor, under the DPWH Ilocos Norte First District Engineering Office, with a target completion date of October 4, 2024. RA Pahati Construction is reportedly owned by the family of Rep. Jhong Ceniza of Pantukan, Davao de Oro — a name that has repeatedly surfaced in infrastructure procurement circles.  Sources familiar with congressional contracting allege that RA Pahati has become a favored builder for Rep. Sandro Marcos, the Ilocos Norte 1st District Representative, allegedly with some help from his chief of staff, said to be a relative of Rep. Ceniza’s wife. Residents and local engineers have raised alarm over the collapse, noting that the structure failed despite relatively moderate river flow in recent weeks. Infrastructure experts point out that proper soil compaction, adequate riprap foundation, and correct steel reinforcement are crucial in river dike construction — all of which appear deficient in the broken sections. The collapse has revived long-circulating allegations about flood control allocations being used as a “cash cow” for certain districts.  RA Pahati, controlled by the Ceniza family, has reportedly bagged billions in contracts across Luzon and Mindanao, despite originating from Davao de Oro. In Ilocos Norte, whispers persist that Rep. Sandro Marcos’ chief of staff — reportedly related by marriage to the Cenizas — has been instrumental in channeling projects to RA Pahati, bypassing stricter vetting.  Political analysts warn this could become a serious governance issue for the presidential son, especially as calls mount for greater transparency in the use of massive DPWH flood control budgets. The incident adds to the growing backlash against multi-billion flood control projects nationwide, long suspected to be overpriced, poorly built, and politically manipulated.  In Congress, several lawmakers — particularly from Mindanao — have been calling out selective investigations that spare politically allied districts while targeting rivals. Observers warn that this Laoag project could become a flashpoint, especially since it sits in the home turf of the President’s son, who is expected to champion good governance but now faces scrutiny over his district’s infrastructure spending. DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. So before anyone points a finger at Davao, perhaps we should remember that flooding is not a problem exclusive to one city. Water does not check political affiliations before it rises. Rain does not ask who you voted for before it pours. And rivers certainly don't read campaign speeches.  But here's where I see Davao differently. Because there is another kind of flooding happening here—one that doesn't destroy homes, close roads, or leave mud behind. Davao floods with culture. Walk through this city and you encounter a living mosaic of Mindanao: Indigenous traditions, migrant communities, different languages, cuisines, beliefs, stories, and histories woven together into one constantly evolving urban tapestry. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. And, of course, we have social-media experts who can apparently repair the entire country using nothing but a smartphone and a Facebook account.  But beneath all the noise is something far more difficult to construct: Character. You can build a highway. You can build skyscrapers. You can build malls, bridges, offices, and massive developments. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. It has to grow. And Davao has grown through people. People from different places came here. They planted roots. They built families. They opened businesses. They raised children. They created communities. And little by little, their individual stories became part of the larger story of the city. For the past 15 years, I have had the privilege of traveling around Davao for team-building activities, retreats, seminars, workshops, and speaking engagements. And in those years, I have seen something that no flood statistics can capture. I have seen people flood others with smiles, generosity, and warmth.
